title: Sort Life by Asking the Right Questions

scenes.tts: A drop of pond water can hold living things from all three domains. A domain is the largest group in classification. You may see algae, an amoeba, and tiny animals. Other specks are too small to make out. How could you sort living things you have never seen before?
scenes.visual: A drop outline holds labelled organisms and specks; three domain names appear beside it; a question mark asks which questions, in what order.
scenes.narration: A drop of pond water can hold living things from all three domains. A domain is the largest group in classification. You may see algae, an amoeba, and tiny animals. Other specks are too small to make out. How could you sort living things you have never seen before?

scenes.tts: The first question is about the nucleus. A nucleus is a compartment wrapped in membrane that holds the D N A. A eukaryote has cells with a nucleus. A prokaryote is a one-celled organism with no nucleus. Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotes. Eukarya are the eukaryotes.
scenes.caption: The first question is about the nucleus. A nucleus is a compartment wrapped in membrane that holds the DNA. A eukaryote has cells with a nucleus. A prokaryote is a one-celled organism with no nucleus. Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotes. Eukarya are the eukaryotes.
scenes.visual: Two cell outlines: one with a nucleus holding a DNA bar, one with the DNA bar and no nucleus; domain names settle under them.
scenes.narration: The first question is about the nucleus. A nucleus is a compartment wrapped in membrane that holds the DNA. A eukaryote has cells with a nucleus. A prokaryote is a one-celled organism with no nucleus. Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotes. Eukarya are the eukaryotes.

scenes.tts: Bacteria and archaea look alike under a light microscope. So we need other evidence. One kind is ribosomal R N A, a molecule every cell uses to build proteins. Its sequence differs between the two. Another is the cell wall. Most bacteria have peptidoglycan in the wall. Archaea walls have none. Only sequence or chemical evidence can tell them apart.

scenes.visual: Two identical cell outlines; two evidence rows fill in for each: RNA sequence pattern and wall peptidoglycan.

Its sequence differs between the two. Another is the cell wall. Most bacteria have peptidoglycan in the wall. Archaea walls have none. Only sequence or chemical evidence can tell them apart.

scenes.tts: Now take a cell with a nucleus. Eukarya have four kingdoms. A kingdom is the rank just below domain. Plants have many cells and cellulose walls. Most plants are autotrophs, which make their own food. Fungi have chitin walls. They are decomposers, which absorb food from dead material. Animals have many cells and no walls. They are ingesters, which take food inside the body. One eukaryotic cell that fits none of these is a protist.
scenes.visual: Four kingdom columns branch from a nucleus-yes box; each gets a small row of cells, wall rings and feeding labels.

scenes.tts: These questions make a dichotomous key. A dichotomous key is a set of paired choices that leads you to a group. A key works only for the organisms and traits built into it. A species also gets a two part name. The genus comes first, with a capital letter. The species comes second, in lower case. The blue crab is Callinectes sapidus.
scenes.visual: The key as a flowchart of paired choices; then the flowchart clears and a two-word scientific name shows genus with capital and species in lower case.

A species also gets a two part name. The genus comes first, with a capital letter. The species comes second, in lower case. The blue crab is Callinectes sapidus.

scenes.tts: So how can we classify an organism we have never seen before? Ask the trait questions in order. Where looks are not enough, check the sequence or chemical evidence. The three domains are branches of one tree, worked out from sequence comparisons. Branches show relatedness, not rank.
scenes.visual: The essential question, two steps that answer it, and a three-branch tree labelled relatedness, not rank.
